introduction.text: **Before you start.** `BAK-2` taught short pastry, cakes, pastry cream and the first tart. This course adds the pastry work most home bakers avoid because it seems difficult, and shows that it is mostly temperature and timing:

items.text: **choux:** a cooked paste leavened by steam, for *éclairs*, profiteroles and savoury *gougères*;
**laminated dough:** how layers of butter and dough rise, made as rough puff for tarts, pies and *palmiers*;
**tarts:** fruit tarts, baked fillings and savoury pies, all with a crisp base;
**creams, ganache and mousses:** *crème anglaise* variations, ganache as an emulsion, mousses set with gelatine or chocolate;
**chocolate:** types, melting without seizing, and tempering by the seed method;
**planning:** a dessert built from components made over three days.

introduction.text: The method follows the CIA's baking and pastry fundamentals [S9]: weighed formulas, temperatures checked with a thermometer, each element judged in cross-section. The fruit is Dutch and seasonal: rhubarb and strawberries in early summer, plums in late summer, apples and pears from autumn. Chocolate, vanilla and citrus are pantry goods.

items.text: pastry cream, custards and *crème anglaise* cooked to at least 71 °C, cooled by the cooling standard, kept at most 2 days;
anything with raw egg made with pasteurised egg for every guest, and kept covered in the fridge for at most 24 hours;
cream fillings kept in the fridge, out of it for at most 2 hours.

introduction.text: Plan five to six weeks. Laminated dough and multi-day desserts need several short sessions over a few days; most bakes are household desserts, or go into the freezer.

**Have ready:** the 1 g scale and the 0.1 g scale; the instant-read thermometer; piping bags with a plain round and a star nozzle; the rolling pin; a tart tin or ring; a metal pie tin of about 22 cm; a heatproof bowl for a bain-marie; the stick blender; glasses, ramekins or rings for mousses; a baking stone or steel (optional); a wire rack; baking paper and baking beans; a pastry brush; the formula sheets; the journal.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PST-3.M1` in the course file, 1 of them a safety item. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** choux is the most surprising dough in pastry: a paste cooked in a pan that puffs into a hollow shell with no yeast or baking powder. Once you can judge the egg, it is quick and reliable.

**You need:** for about 30 small choux: 125 g water, 125 g milk, 110 g butter, 4 g salt, 5 g sugar, 140 g plain flour, about 250 g beaten egg (5 eggs, weighed); a heavy saucepan; a wooden spoon or a stand mixer; a piping bag with a plain round nozzle; baking paper; the scale.
**Explanation:**

*The panade.* Bring the water, milk, butter, salt and sugar to the boil, the butter fully melted. Off the heat, add all the flour at once and stir hard. Back on a medium heat, stir until the paste comes away from the pan and a thin film forms on the bottom, about 2 minutes. Cooking the flour gelatinises the starch, so it can hold the steam later.

*Adding the eggs.* Move the paste to a bowl and let it cool slightly, a few minutes, so the eggs don't cook. Beat in the egg in parts, each part fully absorbed before the next. Stop when the paste is glossy and falls from the spoon in a "V" that holds. The amount varies with how much water evaporated in the pan, so it is judged, not fixed: you may not need all of it.

*Steam leavening.* In a hot oven the water in the paste turns to steam and puffs the shell; the egg proteins and the starch set around the hollow. That is why the oven door stays shut while the shells rise.
*Piping.* A plain round nozzle:

items.text: **rounds:** the bag held upright, close to the tray, squeezed, then stopped and lifted;
**éclairs:** the bag at an angle, piped in even lengths;
**finish:** points smoothed with a wet finger; a thin egg wash.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **The paste (60 min).** A batch of choux paste, the egg added to the "V"; piped into rounds and *éclair* lengths; baked (`PST-3.M1.L2`).
**Consistency (45 min).** One batch split three ways, with too little, just enough and too much egg; baked side by side and photographed.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a film on the pan base;
a glossy "V" off the spoon;
even piping.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: All the egg added at once
Add it in parts; stop at the "V"
Hold back the last egg; judge the "V"
Cool the paste for a few minutes first

blocks.text: **Safety:** the panade is hot and sticky: stir with a long spoon and keep your hand out of the steam. Choux contains gluten, egg and milk (`SAF-1.M4`).
**Record:** the weight of egg used, photos of the "V" and the three consistencies baked.
**Why it matters:** a choux shell is only good if it is hollow, dry and crisp when it reaches the table. Baking, drying and the moment of filling decide that.

**You need:** a batch of choux paste (`PST-3.M1.L1`); pastry cream (`BAK-2.M5`) or whipping cream; dark chocolate for a glaze; aged Gouda for the *gougères*; piping bags; a small nozzle for filling; a wire rack; a serrated knife.
**Explanation:**

*Baking.* A hot oven, around 200 °C, to puff; then turned down to dry and set. Keep the door shut for the first two thirds of the time: open it early and the steam escapes and the shells collapse. They are done when they are golden all over, including the cracks, and feel light for their size.

*Drying out.* Pierce each shell underneath, or split it, and return it to the switched-off oven with the door ajar for 10 minutes, so the inside dries. The result is a hollow, crisp shell that doesn't go soft.
*Gougères.* Beat grated cheese (aged Gouda works well) into the paste, pipe small rounds, top with a little more cheese, and bake. Serve warm, as a starter or with drinks.

*Fillings.* Pastry cream (`BAK-2.M5`), whipped cream, or a *crème diplomate* (pastry cream lightened with whipped cream). Fill close to serving, from underneath with a small nozzle, so the shell stays crisp. Dip the tops in melted chocolate or a glaze.
*Collapse and hollowness:*

items.text: **collapsed shells:** underbaked, the door opened early, or too much egg;
**doughy inside:** not dried out;
**cracked, uneven shells:** the oven too hot or the paste too stiff;
**small and dense:** too little egg, or an oven not hot enough.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **Profiteroles and *éclairs* (75 min).** Baked, dried out, filled with pastry cream, glazed with chocolate.
***Gougères* (60 min).** Cheese choux for a starter; one shell cut in cross-section and photographed.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: golden, light for their size;
hollow and dry inside;
still crisp an hour after filling.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Keep it shut for the first two thirds
Pierce and dry in the cooling oven

blocks.text: **Safety:** cream-filled pastries are kept in the fridge and out of it for at most 2 hours (§9); the pastry cream is cooked to at least 71 °C and cooled by the standard (§9).
**Record:** cross-section photos, the baking times, and the time between filling and serving.

**Task:** make one choux batch serve a savoury and a sweet course, and diagnose a failure. Split the batch: *gougères* with cheese beaten in, and profiteroles filled with pastry cream and glazed with chocolate. Photograph the cross-sections for AI review. Diagnose in writing, from the science, your first failed or weaker bake (from `PST-3.M1.L1` or this one), and correct it in the next bake.
**You need:** the choux formula; aged Gouda; the pastry cream ingredients; dark chocolate; piping bags; a serrated knife; the thermometer; the phone for photos.
**Framework:** the choux formula.

rows: Water and milk, butter, salt, sugar, boiled; flour in at once; cooked to a film
Added in parts to a glossy "V"
Around 200 °C to puff, then lower; door shut for two thirds
Pierced, in the cooling oven, door ajar
Pastry cream (to 71 °C, cooled), close to serving; chocolate glaze
The earlier failure, its cause from the science, the correction

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Make the paste; split; finish both.
Pipe, bake and dry.
Fill the profiteroles close to serving; glaze.
Photograph cross-sections.
Diagnose the earlier failure and record the correction.

blocks.text: **Show:** the choux element of `TS-BAK` level 4 (hollow and crisp), with one failure diagnosed and corrected. The laminated pastry, the tarts, the creams and the chocolate follow in `PST-3.M2.X1`, `PST-3.M3.X1`, `PST-3.M4.X1` and `PST-3.M5.X1`.

AI review reads the cross-sections and the diagnosis: *competent* is hollow, dry shells with an even crust, and a diagnosis that names the cause (egg, steam, drying) and a correction that worked; *not yet* is a doughy centre, or a diagnosis without a cause.
**Time:** 2 h.

items.question: What makes choux rise?

options.text: steam from the water in the paste

items.question: Why is the flour cooked in the *panade*?

options.text: the starch gelatinises so the paste can hold steam

items.question: How do you know enough egg is in?

options.text: by the recipe's number of eggs
the paste is glossy and falls in a "V" that holds

items.question: Your *éclairs* collapsed when they came out. The likeliest cause?

options.text: underbaked, or the door opened early

items.question: Why are choux shells dried out after baking?

options.text: so the inside sets dry and the shell stays crisp

items.question: How long may cream-filled profiteroles stand on the buffet?

options.text: at most 2 hours out of the fridge

items.question: When are profiteroles filled?
Your choux are small, dense and cracked. What do you change?
items.answer: Add a little more egg to a softer "V" and check the oven is hot enough (with the oven thermometer); pipe evenly.
items.why: Too stiff a paste or a cool oven.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** puff pastry rises because of how it is built, not because of an ingredient. Understanding the layers, and the butter temperature that keeps them, makes every laminated dough you will ever make easier.
**You need:** 150 g plain flour; 3 g salt; about 75 g iced water; 100 g cold butter; the rolling pin; a ruler; a sharp knife; cling film; the fridge; a lamp or a window for the photos.
**Explanation:**

*Layers.* A dough and a fat are folded so they form many thin, separate layers. In the oven, the water in the dough and the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart; the gluten holds them; the butter fries them crisp.

*Folds.* Each "turn" multiplies the layers: a letter fold (in thirds, like a letter) triples them. After one turn, three butter layers; after two, nine; after three, twenty-seven. Rough puff uses fewer, quicker turns than classic puff, with the butter in pieces rather than one block.
*Butter temperature.* The butter must be cold and pliable at the same time, about as firm as the dough:

items.text: **too warm:** it melts into the dough and the layers disappear;
**too cold:** it shatters into flakes, and the layers break.

blocks.text: Rests in the fridge between turns keep the butter there and relax the gluten. Press the dough with a finger: it should feel like the butter, cool and firm, with no greasy patches.

*The butter itself.* Butter with a higher fat content, often sold as baking butter, and a waxy texture laminates more easily: it bends rather than breaking, and holds less water to escape. Reason your choice (`IN-DAI`).
*Gluten.* A lean dough with moderate gluten, mixed only until it holds together. Overworked dough shrinks in the oven and turns tough.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Fold and see (60 min).** A small dough laminated with cold butter (the flattened block folded in, as for classic puff), rested, and cut after one, two and three turns; the layers photographed against the light.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: visible, separate layers in the cut;
the butter pliable, not greasy or brittle.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Back in the fridge as soon as it feels greasy
Too cold, or the rests skipped
Let it soften briefly; rest after every turn or two
Dust lightly; brush off the excess

blocks.text: **Safety:** none beyond the kitchen basics: the knife cuts straight down, away from your fingers.
**Record:** the three cut photos, labelled by the number of turns, and a note on the butter's feel.

**Why it matters:** rough puff gives most of the rise of classic puff for a fraction of the work, and it is the dough of the course's pies and *palmiers*. Making it twice, the second time with your own corrections, is how it becomes yours.

**You need:** for about 650 g: 250 g plain flour, 4 g salt, 250 g cold butter (a high-fat baking butter if available), about 125 g iced water; the rolling pin; a ruler; a pastry scraper; cling film; the turn log.
**Explanation:**
*The method:*

items.text: cube the cold butter (or grate it frozen) and mix it loosely into the flour and salt, the pieces left whole;
add the iced water and bring it together to a shaggy dough with visible butter; don't knead;
roll it into a rectangle about three times as long as it is wide;
letter-fold it in thirds; turn it 90°;
roll and fold again; that is two turns;
wrap it and rest it in the fridge for 30 minutes;
repeat, two turns at a time, for four to six turns in total.

blocks.text: *Managing butter temperature.* A cool kitchen, a cold surface, quick work. When the butter shows signs of softening (greasy or sticky patches, butter smearing on the pin), the dough goes straight back into the fridge, even mid-turn. Log each rest and how the butter felt.
*Shape.* Keep the corners square and the thickness even: roll in both directions, not only away from you, and turn the dough rather than the pin.
*Storing.* Wrapped, in the fridge for a day or two; or frozen.
*Shrinkage.* Rest the dough before cutting and again after shaping, so it doesn't shrink in the oven.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A batch of rough puff (90 min active, 4 h in total).** Made with the full number of turns and rests; logged.
**A second batch (60 min).** Made with the corrections from the first; the two compared in a test bake of a few strips.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: streaks of butter in a smooth dough;
square corners and an even thickness.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Too warm, or too large a piece
Patch with flour; chill; cut the butter smaller next time
Roll both ways; turn the dough
Rest after shaping, 20–30 minutes in the fridge

blocks.text: **Safety:** a cold dough needs force: roll from the centre outwards with the weight of your body, not by pressing on the ends of the pin.
**Record:** the turn log (turns, rests, the butter's feel) for both batches, and the corrections.
**Why it matters:** puff pastry is only as good as its cutting and baking. A dragged knife seals the layers; a pale bake leaves them soggy. Both are easy to avoid.

**You need:** a batch of rough puff (`PST-3.M2.L2`); apples or pears; sugar; butter; a beaten egg; a pie filling (leeks and cheese, or mushrooms); a sharp knife or cutters; a baking tray; baking paper; a fork.
**Explanation:**
*Cutting.* A sharp knife or cutter, straight down: dragging or twisting seals the layers at the edge, and they won't rise. Keep the egg wash off the cut edges for the same reason.
*Shapes:*

items.text: **a *tarte fine*:** a thin, free-form tart with a border, topped with sliced apple or pear, butter and sugar;
**a pie lid:** cut to size, sealed onto the rim, with a vent for the steam;
***palmiers*:** the dough rolled out in sugar, both long sides rolled to the middle, sliced and baked;
**cheese straws:** strips with grated cheese, twisted.

blocks.text: *Full rise and colour.* A hot oven, around 200–220 °C, to puff. Bake until deep golden right through, not pale: pale puff is soggy inside. For a tart that should stay flat, dock the base with a fork, or weigh it down with a second tray for part of the bake.
*Savoury and sweet.* An apple or pear *tarte fine*; a leek and cheese pie; a mushroom pie with a puff lid.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Sweet (60 min).** *Palmiers* and an apple *tarte fine*.
**Savoury (60 min).** A pie with a puff lid; the lid cut and photographed in cross-section.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: an even, tall rise;
deep golden and crisp throughout.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Egg wash on the edges, gluing the layers
A tart that puffed into a dome
The base not docked or weighted
Dock it; weight it with a tray

blocks.text: **Safety:** *palmiers* caramelise: the sugar on the tray is hot enough to burn; let them cool on the rack before handling. A pie filling is cold when the lid goes on (`PST-3.M3.L3`).
**Record:** the cross-section photo of the lid, and the baking times and colour of each item.

exercises.title: Rough puff, used for a savoury pie and *palmiers*
exercises.description: Rough puff, used for a savoury pie and *palmiers*.

blocks.text: **Task:** make rough puff with visible, even layers and use it sweet and savoury. Make a batch by the recipe below, with the turns and rests logged and the butter's feel at each rest. Use it for a savoury pie with a puff lid and for *palmiers*, and photograph the cross-sections for AI review. Diagnose in writing a texture fault from your own pastry (for example shrinkage, a tough or greasy dough, collapsed layers), fix it in the next batch, and confirm the fix in a photo. Write why you chose your butter (fat content, temperature).

**You need:** 250 g plain flour; 4 g salt; 250 g cold butter (a high-fat baking butter if available); about 125 g iced water; the pie filling (seasonal vegetables and cheese, or chicken cooked to 75 °C and cooled); sugar for the *palmiers*; a beaten egg; the pie tin; the turn log.
**Recipe:** rough puff, a pie and *palmiers*.

items.text: **Mix:** butter in cubes into the flour and salt; iced water; a shaggy dough with visible butter.
**Turn:** roll to a rectangle, letter-fold, turn 90°, roll and fold again; rest 30 minutes in the fridge; repeat to six turns; log each rest and the butter's feel.
**Rest:** wrapped, at least an hour, or overnight.
**Pie:** a cold filling in the tin, a lid cut straight down, sealed, vented, egg-washed on top only; rested 20 minutes; baked at around 200–220 °C until deep golden.
***Palmiers*:** the trimmings rolled in sugar, rolled from both sides to the middle, sliced, chilled, baked until caramelised.
**Cut and photograph** the lid and a *palmier* in cross-section.
**Diagnose** a fault from this or the session batches; correct it in the next batch; photograph the fixed result.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-BAK` level 4, the laminated element:** visible, even layers in cross-section.
**`SC-STRC` level 4, in part:** a pastry texture fault diagnosed from the science, fixed and confirmed in a photo. The second fault of the row follows with a tart in `PST-3.M3.X1`.
**`IN-DAI` level 4, further evidence:** the butter function for lamination chosen with a reason; the row was met in `GRD-3.M5.X1`.

blocks.text: AI review reads the cross-sections, the log and the diagnosis: *competent* is distinct, even layers through the lid, a turn log with every rest, and a fault fixed with its cause named; *not yet* is a dense lid, or a fix without a cause.
**Time:** 3 h over two days.

items.question: What makes puff pastry rise?

options.text: steam from the water in the dough and butter, pushing the layers apart

items.question: The butter melted into the dough while rolling. What happens in the oven?

options.text: few or no layers: a short, greasy pastry

items.question: Why rest the dough between turns?

options.text: to firm the butter and relax the gluten

items.question: During rolling, greasy patches appear. What do you do?

options.text: wrap it and chill it before continuing

items.question: Why does puff pastry shrink in the oven?

options.text: the gluten wasn't rested after rolling and shaping

items.question: Why is egg wash kept off the cut edges?

options.text: it glues the layers so they can't rise

items.question: Your puff pastry lid is pale and soft inside. What do you change?

options.text: bake longer, until deep golden through

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a fruit tart shows off the season's fruit on a crisp base and a smooth cream. Every component is simple; the art is keeping the base crisp under the cream until it is eaten.

**You need:** sweet pastry (`BAK-2.M3`) for a 22–24 cm tart tin; pastry cream (`BAK-2.M5`); seasonal fruit (strawberries in June, plums in late summer, pears or apples in autumn); apricot jam or a fruit jelly for the glaze; dark chocolate or an egg for sealing; baking paper and baking beans; a pastry brush; the thermometer.
**Explanation:**
*The components:*

items.text: **a case:** sweet pastry blind-baked fully (`BAK-2.M3`);
**a cream:** a layer of pastry cream (`BAK-2.M5`);
**fruit:** fresh, arranged;
**a glaze:** warmed, sieved apricot jam or a fruit jelly, for shine and to keep the fruit from drying.

blocks.text: *Keeping the base crisp.* Bake the case fully, until golden, not pale. Seal it: brush the inside with a thin layer of melted chocolate, or with egg wash returned to the oven for a few minutes. Assemble close to serving.

*The cream.* Cook the pastry cream until it boils and thickens (well past 71 °C), then cool it by the standard (57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours, to 5 °C within 6 hours in total, §9): spread thin on a tray, covered on the surface. Beat it smooth before spreading.
*Fruit arrangement.* Dry the fruit; cut it evenly; arrange it in overlapping rows or circles from the outside in. One or two fruits, not a fruit salad.
*Seasonal choices.* Strawberries in June; plums in late summer; poached pears or apples in autumn and winter. Juicy fruit needs a firmer cream under it.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A fruit tart (90 min active, 4 h in total).** The case blind-baked and sealed; pastry cream made and cooled; assembled and glazed close to serving.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a crisp base when sliced;
neat rows of fruit;
an even shine.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A soggy base under the cream
Bake it golden; seal it with chocolate or egg wash
Dry the fruit; glaze to seal it
Components ahead; assembly on the day

blocks.text: **Safety:** the pastry cream is cooled by the standard and kept at most 2 days; the tart is kept in the fridge and out of it for at most 2 hours (§9). Wash the fruit before cutting.
**Record:** the plan, the cooling times of the cream, and a slice photo showing the base.
**Why it matters:** a baked filling sets in the oven, and judging that set is the whole skill: too soon and it runs, too late and it curdles or cracks.

**You need:** a blind-baked sweet pastry case; for a custard tart: eggs, cream, milk, sugar, vanilla or nutmeg; or for a lemon tart: lemons, eggs, sugar, cream; or for a *frangipane*: butter, sugar, eggs, ground almonds (or a nut-free mix of flour and semolina) and pears or plums; the probe; a wire rack.
**Explanation:**

*Frangipane.* Butter and sugar creamed, eggs beaten in, then ground almonds and a little flour. For a nut-free version, use ground toasted seeds, or a mix of flour and semolina. Spread it in the case, press in sliced pears, plums or apples, and bake until set and golden.

*Custard fillings.* A baked custard (eggs, cream or milk, sugar) poured into a blind-baked case and baked in a low oven, so it sets without bubbling or curdling (`EGG-1`). A lemon tart is the classic sharp version (citrus as a pantry good). Fill the case on the oven shelf, so it doesn't spill on the way.
*Judging the set:*

items.text: **a custard** is set when the edge is firm and the centre wobbles like jelly as a whole, not in waves. Probe the centre: at least 71 °C (the egg-thickened row of §9). It finishes setting as it cools;
**a *frangipane*** is set when a skewer comes out clean and the top springs back.

blocks.text: *Cooling.* At room temperature briefly, on a rack, then into the fridge within the 2-hour limit (§9). Slice it cold, with a hot, dry knife.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A custard tart (90 min).** A baked custard or lemon tart; the set judged by the wobble and the probe; sliced when cold.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a smooth, glossy surface without cracks;
a clean slice.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A low oven; take it out at the wobble
Wobble as a whole, and 71 °C in the centre

blocks.text: **Safety:** the custard reaches at least 71 °C in the centre and goes into the fridge within 2 hours (§9). Almonds are a tree nut (`SAF-1.M4`): the nut-free *frangipane* for an allergic guest, and the tart labelled.
**Record:** the probe reading, the wobble, and a slice photo.
**Why it matters:** a savoury pie is a whole main course in pastry, and the hardest test of a crisp base, because the filling is wet. Four habits solve it.

**You need:** short pastry (`BAK-2.M3`) or rough puff (`PST-3.M2.L2`); leeks or onions; eggs; cream and milk; Gouda or another hard cheese; a cold braise (`SLW-3`) or a vegetable and legume filling; the pie tin; a baking tray or stone to preheat; a beaten egg; the probe.
**Explanation:**
*Savoury fillings:*

items.text: **a *quiche*-style custard** with leeks, onions or greens and cheese;
**a pie filling** of braised meat (`SLW-3`), or vegetables and legumes, cooked and then cooled before it goes in.

blocks.text: *Double-crust pies.* A short or rough-puff base and lid: the lid sealed to the base with water or egg and crimped, vented so the steam escapes, egg-washed on top.
*A crisp base under a wet filling.* Four habits:

items.text: **heat from below:** a blind-baked base, or a metal tin on a preheated tray or stone, baked low in the oven;
**a drier filling:** reduced, drained or thickened;
**a cold filling:** it goes in cold, so it doesn't melt the pastry before the oven sets it;
**patience:** baked until the base is browned, not just the lid.

blocks.text: *The temperatures* (§9):

items.text: meat and poultry fillings are cooked to their §9 figures before they go in, and cooled by the standard;
a pie baked from a cold, cooked filling is baked until the centre is steaming hot throughout (the reheating row);
a *quiche* custard reaches at least 71 °C in the centre (the egg-thickened row).

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **A *quiche*-style tart (60 min).** A blind-baked base; a leek and cheese custard; probed; the base checked when sliced.
**A double-crust pie (75 min).** A cold braised filling under a lid, vented; baked low on a hot tray; the base checked.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a crisp, browned base;
a filling that holds its shape when sliced;
no leaks.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: A preheated tray, low in the oven; blind-bake for a *quiche*
Filling bubbling out at the edges
Cut a vent; seal the rim well

blocks.text: **Safety:** fillings cooked to their §9 figures and cooled by the standard before use; the pie steaming hot in the centre, the *quiche* at 71 °C; leftovers in the fridge within 2 hours, kept at most 2 days (§9).
**Record:** the probe readings and the base photos for both.

Diagnose and fix the texture fault; photograph the fixed result.

blocks.text: **Show:** the tart element of `TS-BAK` level 4 and one adapted formula; the second texture fault of `SC-STRC` level 4, recorded with the row of `PST-3.M2` (this module does not move `SC-STRC`).

AI review reads the slice photo, the adaptation and the diagnosis: *competent* is a crisp, golden base under the cream, an adaptation with its reason, and a fault fixed with its cause; *not yet* is a soggy base, or an adaptation without a reason.

exercises.title: A savoury pie for a dinner

blocks.text: **Task:** bake a savoury pie as the main of a dinner, with a crisp base and a filling that holds.

items.text: **The brief:** a savoury pie for the household or guests, in short or rough-puff pastry, with a braised or vegetable filling.
**The constraints:** the filling cooked to its §9 figure and cold when it goes in; vented; baked low on a hot tray.
**The criteria:** the base crisp in a slice photo; the centre steaming hot throughout; household cards.
**The record:** the plan, the probe reading in the centre, the slice photo and the cards.

blocks.text: **You need:** the pastry; the filling (for example the braise of `SLW-3.M2.X1`, or leeks, mushrooms and lentils); the pie tin; a baking tray or stone; a beaten egg; the probe; the household cards.
*Procedure:*

items.text: Plan the pie and the steps towards a crisp base.
Assemble with a cold filling; vent; bake low on a hot tray.
Check the centre; slice; photograph the base.

blocks.text: **Show:** a second tart element of `TS-BAK` level 4: a savoury pie with a crisp base under a wet filling, to standard.

AI review reads the slice photo and the plan: *competent* is a browned, crisp base that holds its shape under the filling, and a plan that names the four habits; *not yet* is a pale or wet base, or a filling that runs.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PST-3.M4` in the course file, 2 of them safety items. Pass mark 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** *crème anglaise* is the mother of pastry creams: a sauce on its own, the base of a *bavarois* and a chocolate *crémeux*, and the ice-cream base of `PST-4`. Infused and scaled with confidence, it opens all of them.

**You need:** for about 600 g: 250 g milk, 250 g cream, 6 yolks (about 110 g), 100 g sugar; a vanilla pod, or a herb (bay, lemon verbena, thyme), coffee beans or tea; a heavy saucepan; a spatula; a sieve; a bowl set in iced water; the thermometer.
**Explanation:**

*The base* (`EGG-1.M4`). Bring the milk and cream to a simmer. Whisk the yolks and sugar until pale. Pour a little hot milk onto the yolks, whisking, then return it all to the pan. Stir over gentle heat, the spatula reaching every corner, until the custard reaches *nappe*: it coats the spatula and a finger drawn through it leaves a clean line. That is around 80–82 °C, well above the 71 °C the egg-thickened row of §9 asks for. Never boil it: at boiling the yolks curdle. Strain it at once into a bowl set in iced water, and stir it as it cools.

*Infusions.* Infuse the milk before the yolks go in: bring it to a simmer with the flavouring, cover it, leave it for 10–30 minutes, and strain it. Vanilla, coffee beans, tea, herbs (bay, lemon verbena, thyme), toasted seeds, citrus zest. Taste the milk: it should taste a little too strong, because the eggs and cream soften it.
*Variations:*

items.text: **a *bavarois*:** *crème anglaise* set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream;
**a chocolate *crémeux*:** hot *crème anglaise* poured over chopped chocolate and blended;
**an ice-cream base** (`PST-4`).

blocks.text: *Scaling.* A larger batch takes longer to thicken and to cool. The cooling standard applies (§9): from 57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours, and to 5 °C or below within 6 hours in total. A double batch cools in two bowls in the ice bath, or in a shallow tray. Keep it covered in the fridge for at most 2 days.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Two infusions (45 min).** A vanilla and a herb *crème anglaise*, to *nappe* with the thermometer; cooled over ice.
**A double batch (45 min).** The same base doubled; the time to *nappe* and the cooling logged.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: *nappe* at about 80–82 °C;
no curdling;
cooled over ice within the limits.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Off the heat at 82 °C; blend at once to rescue a slight curdle
Left to cool in the pan
Strain straight into a bowl over ice

blocks.text: **Safety:** at least 71 °C on the probe; cooled by the standard and logged; at most 2 days in the fridge (§9).
**Record:** the temperatures, the time to *nappe*, and the cooling log for the double batch.
**Why it matters:** ganache is two ingredients and one ratio, and it covers glazes, fillings, truffles and whipped toppings. Seeing it as an emulsion explains why it splits and how to bring it back.
**You need:** 400 g dark chocolate (60–70 %), chopped; 300 g cream; a little warm milk; three bowls; a spatula; the stick blender; the scale.
**Explanation:**
*Ganache as an emulsion.* Chocolate (cocoa butter and cocoa solids) and cream (water and milk fat) are emulsified into a smooth, glossy mass. The ratio sets its use:

items.text: about **1 part chocolate to 1 part cream** (dark chocolate) for a glaze;
about **2 to 1** for a firmer filling and truffles;
**more cream** for a whipped ganache;
milk and white chocolate need more chocolate for the same firmness, because they contain less cocoa solids.

blocks.text: *Making it.* Pour hot cream over the chopped chocolate and leave it for a minute. Stir from the centre outwards in small circles until an emulsion forms in the middle, then widen the circles. Or blend it with a stick blender, the head kept below the surface so no air goes in.

*Fixing a split ganache.* Oily and grainy means the fat has separated. Blend a spoon of warm milk or cream in from the centre, and it comes back. A ganache that is too hot or overworked splits most easily.
*Which chocolate.* A real chocolate of 60–70 %, not compound chocolate: compound coating has other fats instead of cocoa butter, and a waxy texture (`PST-3.M5.L1`).
**Practice:**

items.text: **Three ganaches (60 min).** Glaze (1 : 1), filling (2 : 1) and truffle ratios with dark chocolate, weighed; the textures compared when cool.
**Split and fix (30 min).** A ganache split on purpose (too hot, or over-stirred) and repaired; photographed at each step.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: glossy and smooth;
the ratio matching its use;
the repair photographed.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Cream just off the boil; blend in warm milk to rescue
Stir from the centre; blender head under the surface

blocks.text: **Safety:** ganache contains milk; most chocolate is labelled "may contain" nuts or milk (`SAF-1.M4`): read the label for allergic guests. A ganache with cream is kept in the fridge.
**Record:** the three ratios and their textures, and the split-and-repair photos.
**Why it matters:** a mousse is three parts held in balance: a flavoured base, a foam, and something to set it. Written as a ratio, it can be made with any season's fruit, and varied on purpose.

**You need:** dark chocolate; cream; a seasonal fruit purée (cooked rhubarb, strawberries or plums, sieved); sugar; leaf gelatine; the 0.1 g scale; a whisk or mixer; a large spatula; glasses or rings; the fridge.
**Explanation:**
*The three parts:*

items.text: **a flavoured base:** melted chocolate, a fruit purée, or a *crème anglaise*;
**aeration:** whipped cream, whisked egg whites or an Italian meringue;
**a setting agent:** the chocolate itself, or gelatine.

blocks.text: *Two starting ratios:*

items.text: **chocolate:** 1 part dark chocolate to 2 parts cream by weight; a third of the cream heated and made into a ganache with the chocolate, the rest whipped to soft peaks and folded in;
**fruit:** purée and whipped cream in roughly equal weights, sweetened to taste, set with gelatine.

blocks.text: *Folding.* Fold the foam into the base in thirds, the first third stirred in to loosen it, the rest folded with a large spatula, turning the bowl. Base and foam at compatible temperatures: the chocolate base just warm, so it doesn't seize; the gelatine base cool and starting to thicken, so it doesn't set in strings.
*Gelatine:*

items.text: **blooming:** sheets soaked in cold water and squeezed; or powder sprinkled over a measured cold liquid;
**dosing by weight:** a percentage of the liquid it sets. Sheets differ in strength, so weigh them: take your pack's dose for a soft set, convert it to grams per 100 g of liquid, and log it;
**setting and melting:** gelatine dissolves in warm liquid (never boiled), sets in the fridge over hours, and melts again close to body temperature, which gives the melt-in-the-mouth texture;
**enzymes:** fresh pineapple and kiwi stop it setting unless cooked first;
**origin:** gelatine comes from pork or beef, which matters for vegetarians and some faiths (`NUT-3`).

blocks.text: *Raw egg.* A mousse aerated with egg whites or with yolks that are not cooked is made with pasteurised egg for every guest and kept covered in the fridge for at most 24 hours (§9). A mousse on a cooked base (a *crème anglaise* to 71 °C) and cream keeps at most 2 days. The two ratios above use no raw egg.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A chocolate mousse (60 min active, 4 h in total).** Chocolate as the setting agent; folded; set in glasses.
**A fruit mousse (60 min active, 4 h in total).** A seasonal purée with gelatine dosed by weight and whipped cream; set in rings and unmoulded.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: light and smooth, no streaks of white;
set enough to hold a spoon's shape, melting in the mouth.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Boiled, or added to a cold base
Dissolve it in warm purée; fold when the base is cool
Fold in thirds with a large spatula
Weigh the gelatine; log the dose

blocks.text: **Safety:** raw-egg mousses with pasteurised egg only, at most 24 hours; cream mousses in the fridge, out of it for at most 2 hours (§9). Gelatine is an animal product: tell guests.
**Record:** both ratios as weighed, the gelatine dose, and photos of the set mousses.

rows: 1 part chocolate to 2 parts cream; a third as ganache, the rest whipped
Purée and whipped cream about equal; gelatine by weight
One ratio changed on purpose; the effect recorded
No raw egg, or pasteurised egg with a 24-hour limit

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `PST-3.M5` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** chocolate behaves differently by type, and a few degrees or a drop of water decide whether it stays glossy or turns to grit. Reading the label is the first skill.

**You need:** dark, milk and white chocolate; a dark couverture and a compound (coating) chocolate to compare; a heatproof bowl and a pan for a bain-marie, or a microwave; a dry spatula; the thermometer; the ingredients for a simple brownie or ganache, twice.
**Explanation:**
*Types:*

items.text: **cocoa content:** the percentage of cocoa solids and cocoa butter together. More means more bitter and intense;
**couverture:** extra cocoa butter, so it flows well; for tempering and coating;
**compound chocolate** (coating chocolate): some or all of the cocoa butter replaced by other fats. It needs no tempering, but it has a waxy texture and less flavour;
**dark, milk and white:** milk and white chocolate contain milk solids and more sugar, and they burn and seize more easily.

blocks.text: *Reading a label.* The cocoa percentage; the fats in the ingredients list (cocoa butter only, or vegetable fats too); the milk solids; the allergen line ("may contain nuts").

*Melting without burning.* Chop the chocolate evenly. Melt it over a bain-marie of barely simmering water, the bowl not touching the water, or in short bursts in the microwave, stirring between them. Dark chocolate no hotter than about 50 °C; milk and white lower.

*Seizing.* A few drops of water, or steam from the pan, make melted chocolate thick and grainy. Prevent it with dry bowls and tools, and with the water barely simmering. A seized chocolate is not wasted: it can still go into a ganache or a sauce with more liquid.

*A comparison bake.* The same brownie or ganache made with two chocolates (for example a 70 % couverture and a compound chocolate, or dark and milk), photographed in cross-section and explained: gloss, texture, flavour, set.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Melt and compare (60 min).** Dark, milk and white chocolate melted and their temperatures logged; couverture and compound tasted and compared; the comparison bake made with two chocolates, photographed in cross-section and explained.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: smooth and glossy melted chocolate;
no grain;
you can read a chocolate label and say what it means for the dish.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Steam or water in the bowl
Dry tools; the water barely simmering; use it in a ganache
A microwave run for two minutes
A gentler heat; take it off early and stir

blocks.text: **Safety:** the bain-marie's steam burns: lift the bowl with a cloth, tilting it away from you. Chocolate allergen lines (`SAF-1.M4`) are read for every guest.
**Record:** the melting temperatures, the label notes and the comparison photos with your explanation.

**Why it matters:** tempered chocolate snaps, shines and releases from a mould; untempered chocolate sets dull and soft. The seed method makes tempering possible at home with a bowl and a thermometer.

**You need:** about 500 g of dark couverture, two thirds chopped coarsely and one third chopped finely; a heatproof bowl and a pan; a dry spatula; the thermometer; strips of baking paper; a knife; a cool room.
**Explanation:**

*Why tempering matters.* Cocoa butter can set in several crystal forms; only one (form V) gives a glossy surface, a clean snap, a shrinkage that releases from moulds, and stability at room temperature. Untempered chocolate sets dull and streaky (bloom) and soft.
*The seed method:*

items.text: melt two thirds of the chocolate fully: dark to about 45–50 °C;
stir in the remaining third, finely chopped, as "seed" crystals already in the right form;
stir until it cools to the working temperature: dark about 31–32 °C, milk about 29–30 °C, white about 28–29 °C. The maker's figures on the pack take precedence;
remove any unmelted seed.

blocks.text: *Testing.* Dip a knife tip or a strip of baking paper and leave it at room temperature. Tempered chocolate sets glossy and snaps within a few minutes; untempered stays soft or sets streaky.
*Keeping it in temper.* Work at the working temperature. If it thickens as it cools, warm it briefly over the bain-marie, a few seconds at a time, stirring, without going above the working range.
*The room.* A cool, dry kitchen without a draught or a fan blowing on the chocolate: humidity and cold air both spoil the surface.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Temper dark chocolate (60 min).** By the seed method with a thermometer; tested on a strip; used for dipping (orange peel, biscuits, the profiteroles' tops).
**Temper again (60 min).** A second batch, logged, used for a few simple bars or shards on baking paper.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the test strip glossy and snapping;
the temperatures logged;
no streaks.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The melt overheated, or no seed
Start again: melt fully, seed, cool to the working range
A batch that fails on the bars
Test a strip before using it
A grey bloom on the surface
A cold, humid room, or a fan
Work in a cool, dry room without a draught

blocks.text: **Safety:** keep the chocolate bowl dry and clear of the steam; nothing else beyond the bain-marie's heat.
**Record:** the temperature log for each batch (melt, seed, working), and photos of the strip and the bars.

exercises.title: Temper chocolate twice with the seed method
exercises.description: Temper chocolate twice with the seed method; photograph the snap and shine.

blocks.text: **Task:** temper chocolate reliably, and explain the chocolate types by a comparison. Temper chocolate twice by the seed method, with a temperature log for each batch; photograph the snap and the shine; use one batch to dip or coat. File the comparison bake of `PST-3.M5.L1` (two chocolates in one formula), photographed in cross-section and explained in writing.
**You need:** about 500 g of dark couverture per batch; the thermometer; a heatproof bowl and a pan; baking paper; a knife; something to dip; the comparison bake's photos and notes.
**Recipe:** the seed method.

items.text: **Chop** the couverture: two thirds coarsely, one third finely.
**Melt** the two thirds over barely simmering water, stirring, to 45–50 °C; log it.
**Seed:** off the heat, stir in the finely chopped third.
**Cool** to 31–32 °C, stirring (or the maker's figure on the pack); log it; remove any unmelted seed.
**Test** a strip; if it sets glossy and snaps within a few minutes, it is in temper; log it.
**Use** it: dip, coat, or pour into bars; keep it at the working temperature, warming briefly if needed.
**Photograph** the snap and the shine.
**Repeat** with a second batch on another day.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`TS-BAK` level 4, the chocolate part:** tempered chocolate with snap and shine, logged twice.
**`IN-BAK` level 3:** the items at 80 % and a comparison bake photographed in cross-section and explained.

blocks.text: AI review reads the logs and the photos: *competent* is two batches with every temperature logged in range, a glossy surface and a clean snap, and a comparison explained by the ingredients; *not yet* is a streaky or soft set, or a log with missing temperatures.
**Time:** 2 h.

items.question: What does the percentage on a dark chocolate bar mean?

options.text: cocoa solids and cocoa butter together

items.question: What is compound chocolate?

options.text: chocolate in which other fats replace some cocoa butter; no tempering needed

items.question: Melted chocolate turns thick and grainy after steam got in. What happened?
Which chocolate burns most easily?

options.text: so cocoa butter sets in the crystal form that gives shine, snap and stability

items.question: In the seed method, what does the chopped chocolate do?

options.text: cools and seeds the right crystals

options.text: a dipped knife tip or paper strip sets glossy and snaps within minutes

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none for this module. Its storage rules were checked in `PST-3.M3` and `PST-3.M4`.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** a dessert of four components made on the day is a stressful afternoon; the same dessert planned over three days is an easy assembly. Planning backwards from serving is how pastry kitchens work, and it works at home.
**You need:** the dessert you will make in `PST-3.M6.X1`; a three-day planning sheet; labels; containers; fridge and freezer space; the cooling log.
**Explanation:**
*Working backwards.* Start from the moment of serving and place each component on the day it is best made, given how long it keeps:

items.text: **doughs** (short, rough puff): days ahead, chilled or frozen;
**baked cases:** a day ahead, airtight;
**creams and curds:** a day ahead, cooled by the standard, in the fridge;
**mousses:** the day before, because they need hours to set; a raw-egg mousse no more than 24 hours ahead (§9);
**glazes, tempered decorations and fruit:** on the day;
**assembly:** at the last moment.

blocks.text: *Storage per component.* Each gets a container, a label with the date, a place (fridge or freezer), and a quality limit. For example: a baked case goes soft after two days; a pastry cream is used within 2 days (§9).
*Control points:*

items.text: the cooling of creams and custards (57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours, to 5 °C within 6 hours in total, §9);
the fridge at 4 °C;
the time out of the fridge on the day, at most 2 hours.

blocks.text: *A plan against actual.* Write the planned time for each step; log the actual time beside it; note the slips and why they happened. The next plan starts from those notes.
*An example, a plum tart with chocolate for Saturday:*

items.text: **Thursday:** sweet pastry made and chilled; pastry cream made and cooled;
**Friday:** the case blind-baked and sealed; plums poached;
**Saturday:** chocolate tempered for shards; the tart assembled and glazed an hour before serving.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **Plan and run (90 min of planning and logging, 2 days in total).** The plan of `PST-3.M6.X1` written and followed, with every component's day, storage and control point.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: every component placed on a day with its storage;
nothing made on the day that should have been made earlier.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Plan backwards; move what keeps to earlier days
At most 2 days; label with the date

blocks.text: **Safety:** the creams' cooling is logged; components are labelled and dated; nothing is out of the fridge for more than 2 hours on the day (§9).
**Record:** the plan, the actual times beside it, and the notes on the slips.

blocks.text: **Task:** plan and make a multi-component dessert across three days, serving it on time.

items.text: **The brief:** a plated or assembled dessert for six guests with at least four components from this course (for example a pastry base, a cream or mousse, a fruit element and a chocolate decoration), made over three days.
**The constraints:**
a written plan with control points: cooling, storage, time out of the fridge;
allergens and risk groups asked about in advance (raw egg only as pasteurised egg, within 24 hours).
**The criteria:** the plan against the actual times logged; every control point met, or a change reasoned; guest cards.
**The record:** the plan, the log, photos of each component and the dessert, the cards and your review.

blocks.text: **You need:** the components' ingredients; seasonal Dutch fruit; labels and containers; the thermometer; the planning sheet; the guest cards.
*Procedure:*

items.text: Write the three-day plan with storage and control points.
Make the components on their days; log the times and control points.
Assemble and serve; photograph; guest cards.
Compare plan and actual; note the changes.

blocks.text: **Show:** a multi-day plan with control points, the log showing every control point met or a reasoned change. This meets the `KM-PLAN` level 4 row, as `FIR-3.M6.X1` does for a live-fire meal.

AI review reads the plan and the log: *competent* is four components on reasoned days, every cooling and storage point logged, and the dessert served on time; *not yet* is a missing control point, or components made on the day without a reason.
**Time:** 4 h over three days.
